q: What does the communications management plan describe?
options: The order in which work packages will be completed and handed over
The criteria that the sponsor will use to accept the final deliverables
How, when and by whom information is administered and disseminated
The budget that is reserved for buying communication technology
explanation: The communications management plan describes how, when and by whom information will be administered and disseminated, and how communications will be planned, structured, implemented and monitored.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Communications management plan

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Communications management plan

q: Which of these items does the communications management plan include?
options: The person responsible for authorizing release of confidential information
The salary bands of the people who prepare and send the project reports
The detailed technical design of every deliverable the project team produces
The full list of risks with their probability and impact ratings
explanation: The plan includes stakeholder requirements, information to be communicated, escalation processes, reasons, timeframe and frequency, the person responsible for communicating, the person responsible for authorizing release of confidential information, recipients, and methods.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Communications management plan

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Communications management plan

q: A project team has 10 members, including the project manager. How many potential communication channels are there?
explanation: Channels = N × (N − 1) / 2. Here 10 × 9 / 2 = 45.
ref: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 11, Q18

links.label: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 11, Q18

q: A team of 8 people grows to 10. How many communication channels are added?
explanation: Before: 8 × 7 / 2 = 28 channels. After: 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 channels. Added: 45 − 28 = 17.
ref: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 11, Q18

links.label: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 11, Q18

q: The project manager emails a monthly report to 40 stakeholders. Which communication method is this?
options: Interactive communication
Pull communication
Push communication
Verbal communication
explanation: Push communications are sent or distributed directly to specific recipients who need the information, for example letters, memos, reports and emails.

q: What is the main limitation of push communication, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: It ensures distribution but not that the message is understood
It can only be used for small, simple information sets
It requires every recipient to be present at exactly the same time
It cannot be used for reports or press releases
explanation: Push communication ensures that the information is distributed but does not ensure that it reaches or is understood by the intended audience.

q: A program has thousands of users who need extensive training content, to be used whenever they choose. Which communication method fits best?
options: Interactive communication
Push communication
Small group communication
Pull communication
explanation: Pull communication is used for large, complex information sets or for large audiences; recipients access content at their own discretion, for example eLearning courses and web portals.

q: In the basic communication model, what is the step in which the message is coded into symbols such as text or sound?
options: Decode
Encode
Acknowledge
Feedback
explanation: The basic model is encode (code the message into symbols), transmit (send it through a channel, where noise may interfere) and decode (the receiver translates it back into a useful form).

q: A stakeholder acknowledges receipt of a message. What does this mean in the interactive communication model?
options: The stakeholder agrees with the message
The stakeholder has fully understood everything in the message
The message was received, not necessarily understood
The sender no longer needs any feedback
explanation: Acknowledging receipt does not necessarily mean agreement with or comprehension of the message, merely that it has been received. Understanding is confirmed through feedback.

q: In the communication model, what is the sender responsible for?
options: Making the message clear and complete, and confirming it is understood
Only transmitting the message through whatever channel the plan has chosen
Decoding the message into a form that is useful to the receiver
Acknowledging receipt of the message on behalf of the receiver
explanation: The sender is responsible for transmitting the message, ensuring the information is clear and complete, and confirming the message is correctly interpreted. The receiver decodes, interprets and acknowledges or responds.

q: Which of these is an example of noise in the communication model?
options: The receiver's acknowledgment that the message arrived
The sender's encoding of the message
Feedback that matches the original message
The receiver's distraction or lack of interest
explanation: Noise includes any interference or barriers that might compromise understanding of the message, such as the distraction of the receiver, variations in perception, or lack of knowledge or interest.

q: A stakeholder says she never understood a key decision, although it was emailed to her twice. What should the project manager do?
options: Email it a third time, this time marked with a high-priority flag
Check her needs and use a method with feedback, such as a short call
Record that she was informed, and close the matter in the issue log today
Ask the sponsor to remind her that she needs to read her emails
explanation: Push communication such as email ensures distribution, not understanding. The interactive model adds feedback to confirm understanding, and communication should be tailored to the stakeholder's needs.

q: What does the Monitor Communications process ensure?
options: That every stakeholder receives exactly the same report each month
That the communication budget is never once exceeded during the project
That the information needs of the project and stakeholders are met
That all communication between stakeholders is put in writing
explanation: Monitor Communications is the process of ensuring the information needs of the project and its stakeholders are met; its key benefit is the optimal information flow defined in the communications and stakeholder engagement plans.

q: What is the purpose of a visual control, or information radiator, such as a task board?
options: To let anyone compare actual with expected performance at a glance
To store confidential documents for the steering committee's review
To replace the product backlog as the team's list of future work
To record each member's working hours for the finance department
explanation: Visual controls illustrate processes so that actual and expected performance can easily be compared. They should be highly visible for anyone to see; a task board shows work to do, in progress and completed.

q: An agile team is choosing metrics for its dashboard. What does the Agile Practice Guide advise?
options: Track every single metric that the team's tools are able to produce
Hide the metrics until they start to show good results
Change the whole set of metrics in every single iteration
Start small and drop metrics that no longer inform decisions
explanation: The measurement guidelines: start small with a minimal set of metrics, visualize openly, review and act on them, and decommission metrics that no longer influence decisions.

q: A sponsor asks an agile team when the remaining scope will be finished. How should the team report this?
options: As a single fixed date that the whole team will commit to meeting
As a probabilistic forecast, such as a range with a confidence level
As the total number of hours each team member has worked so far
As a refusal, since agile teams never forecast any of their delivery dates
explanation: Stable throughput and an up-to-date item count allow probabilistic forecasts. Teams should present forecasts as ranges or confidence curves, never as single-point commitments.

q: How should project information be reported to different groups of stakeholders?
options: With the same detailed report sent to every group
Only by exception, when something goes wrong
Adapted in level, format and detail to each group
Only through formal presentations to the sponsor
explanation: Project information is distributed to many groups and should be adapted to provide an appropriate level, format and detail for each type of stakeholder. It may be prepared regularly or on an exception basis.

q: What does a status report typically include, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Progress since the last report and forecasts for cost and schedule
The full list of requirements and the acceptance criteria for each
The team's values, agreements and operating guidelines for working
The contracts signed with each supplier and the payments made to them
explanation: A status report provides information on the current status of the project and may include progress since the last report and forecasts for cost and schedule performance.

q: A project dashboard shows a red stoplight for one measure. What does the PMBOK Guide suggest adding?
options: A second dashboard version that hides the red measure
A new baseline so that the measure turns green again
Nothing, because the colors speak clearly for themselves
A text explanation for measures outside the thresholds
explanation: Dashboards often use stoplight (red-amber-green) charts, bar charts, pie charts and control charts; a text explanation can be used for any measures outside the established thresholds.

q: What are work performance reports intended to generate?
options: Contracts, invoices and payments
Decisions, actions or awareness
Requirements and acceptance criteria
Team charters and ground rules
explanation: Work performance reports are representations of work performance information intended to generate decisions, actions or awareness, circulated as the communications management plan defines.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Work performance reports

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Work performance reports

q: Which of these is a leading indicator that project performance may be at risk?
options: The cost variance that was reported last month
The number of deliverables that are already completed
Key stakeholders who are not available or engaged
The resources consumed during the last phase
explanation: Leading indicators give early warning: the lack of a risk management process, stakeholders who are not available or engaged, or poorly defined success criteria. Cost variance, deliverables completed and resources consumed are lagging indicators.

q: Why does the PMBOK Guide prefer leading indicators whenever possible?
options: They can help prevent problems before variances cross thresholds
They are always much easier to measure than lagging indicators
They remove the need to track any lagging indicators at all
They are needed only on predictive projects, never on agile ones
explanation: Leading indicators reveal trends before performance variances cross the tolerance threshold, so they can be used to prevent problems that may require rework. Lagging indicators are easier to measure.

q: Which is one of the three core components of effective project governance in the PMBOK Guide?
options: A fixed meeting schedule that every project in the portfolio follows
A single report format that is used for all of the stakeholders
Approval of every single task by the steering committee, in advance
Signaling mechanisms, such as leading indicators, for target metrics
explanation: Effective governance requires target metrics aligned with strategic goals, clear signaling mechanisms or alarm systems for those metrics (typically leading indicators), and effective feedback mechanisms for decision-makers.

q: This iteration burndown chart will go into the iteration report. Which statement about it is accurate?
options: The team completed all 50 story points by the last day
Remaining work rose on day 7, and 4 points were left at the end
The team stayed ahead of the ideal line for most of the iteration
Remaining work fell by the same amount every single day
explanation: Remaining work went from 27 points on day 6 to 31 on day 7, so work was added or re-estimated, and 4 points were still open on day 10. The actual line was above the ideal line, that is behind it, after day 0.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Work performance reports

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Work performance reports

q: How should governance, including its reporting, be tailored according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Comprehensive for every project, whatever its approach
Left out entirely for adaptive and hybrid projects
Lighter for adaptive work, fuller for large predictive work
Decided by each team member individually for their own tasks
explanation: Governance can be tailored: lightweight for adaptive methods, moderate or combined for hybrid projects, and comprehensive for large predictive portfolios, programs and projects.

q: Which THREE does communication requirements analysis consider, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: The number of potential communication channels
Legal requirements
Internal and external information needs
The team members' hourly rates
The make-or-buy decision
The critical path of the schedule
explanation: Sources include the stakeholder register and engagement plan, the number of communication channels, organizational charts, relationships, the development approach, disciplines involved, logistics, internal and external information needs, and legal requirements.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Communication requirements analysis

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Communication requirements analysis

q: Which TWO are examples of pull communication?
options: Web portals
Knowledge repositories
Emails
Press releases
Phone calls
explanation: Pull methods include web portals, intranet sites, eLearning courses, lessons learned databases and knowledge repositories. Emails and press releases are push; phone calls are interactive.

q: Which TWO are measurement guidelines in the Agile Practice Guide?
options: Visualize openly on information radiators or dashboards
Decommission metrics that no longer influence decisions
Collect every metric the tools can produce
Show the metrics only to the project manager
Change the metric set in every iteration
explanation: The four guidelines are: start small and evolve; visualize openly; review and act; decommission low-value metrics.

q: Match each form of communication with its description.
right: Between individuals, typically face to face
Within groups of three to six people
A speaker addressing a larger audience
Minimal connection to a large, sometimes anonymous audience
explanation: The communications management plan applies different approaches to interpersonal, small group, public and mass communication.

q: Complete each statement with the communication method it describes.

blanks.text: A videoconference with the design team is
A weekly report emailed to the sponsor is
A lessons learned database searched when needed is

explanation: Interactive: real-time, multidirectional, such as meetings and videoconferencing. Push: sent to specific recipients, such as reports and emails. Pull: accessed at the recipient's discretion, such as lessons learned databases.
